title: Ancient Egyptian
description: The three seasons of the ancient Egyptian civil year, with the epagomenal days stretched into a month
origin: The Egyptian civil calendar had three seasons of four months, each of 30 days, plus five extra days at the end of the year, 365 in all. Egyptologists number the months, such as Akhet I, because the names used in daily life came from festivals. The year had no leap day, so it drifted against the seasons and the star Sirius until the Canopus decree tried to add one. Ancient Egypt never had a 13th month: here the five extra days, Heriu Renpet, are stretched to a full month, and the order is rotated to start with Shemu so that the extra days fall between the harvest and the flood.

leapWeek.name: Leap week
leapWeek.meaning: The civil calendar had no leap day, so it slipped by about one day every four years. In 238 BC the Canopus decree of Ptolemy III ordered a sixth extra day every fourth year, but the priests resisted and it was dropped. Augustus finally made it stick in 26 or 25 BC. This calendar adds a whole week instead.

months.name: Shemu I
months.meaning: The first month of Shemu, the harvest season, when the Nile was low and the grain was cut. It was the ninth month of the civil year. Months came to be named after festivals, but Egyptologists number them by season.

months.name: Shemu II
months.meaning: The second month of Shemu, the harvest season. Egyptologists number the months within each season.

months.name: Shemu III
months.meaning: The third month of Shemu, the harvest season.

months.name: Shemu IV
months.meaning: The last month of Shemu, and of the civil year. Its Greek name, Mesore, comes from Mesut Ra, "birth of Ra". It was also called Wep Renpet, "opening of the year".

months.name: Heriu Renpet
months.meaning: The five extra days at the end of the civil year, celebrated as the birthdays of Osiris, Horus, Set, Isis and Nephthys, and considered dangerous. Egyptians treated them as outside the year proper.
months.notes: The 13th month. In Egypt it was only five days long; here it is stretched to 28. It sits where the real extra days fell, between the last Shemu month and Akhet I, the month of the Sirius flood.

months.name: Akhet I
months.meaning: The first month of Akhet, the inundation, when the Nile flooded the fields. In the ideal calendar the year began here, with the rising of Sirius.

months.name: Akhet II
months.meaning: The second month of Akhet, the inundation season.

months.name: Akhet III
months.meaning: The third month of Akhet, the inundation season.

months.name: Akhet IV
months.meaning: The last month of Akhet, the inundation season.

months.name: Peret I
months.meaning: The first month of Peret, the season of emergence or growth, when the land came out of the floodwater and was sown.

months.name: Peret II
months.meaning: The second month of Peret, the season of emergence or growth.

months.name: Peret III
months.meaning: The third month of Peret, the season of emergence or growth.

months.name: Peret IV
months.meaning: The last month of Peret, the season of emergence or growth, just before the harvest.
